extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means-/step-plus-function), how to apply the three‑prong test, the disclosure requirements for corresponding structure, and special rules for computer‑implemented limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption: 'means' or 'step' invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) when it explicitly uses the term "means" or "step" and includes functional language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure, material or acts necessary to perform the recited function (see TriMed v. Stryker). If the examiner determines that 'means' or 'step' is used but the second or third prong is not met, the Office action must explain why the limitation using 'means' or 'step' is not being treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f). Examiners should expressly state in the Office action when 112(f) is being applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-prong analysis to determine 112(f) applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation only if it meets this 3-prong analysis: (A) the claim limitation uses the term 'means' or 'step' or a generic placeholder (a substitute for 'means'); (B) the term is modified by functional language (typically linked by 'for' or similar); and (C) the term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three prongs are cumulative. Functional linking words include 'for', 'so that', 'configured to', etc. If unclear whether a limitation falls within 112(f), the examiner should evaluate all prongs and state the conclusion. Applicants can rebut by showing sufficient structure or amending the claim to avoid 112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttable presumption when 'means'/'step' not present
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation that does not use the term 'means' or 'step' triggers the rebuttable presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should nonetheless consider whether the presumption is overcome (e.g., where a generic placeholder is used or the term 'fails to recite sufficiently definite structure' or else 'recites function without reciting sufficient structure' as in Williamson). Case law (Phillips, CCS Fitness, Personalized Media, Williamson) guides this inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic placeholders that may invoke 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain non-structural generic placeholders (terms that are substitutes for 'means') may invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f), e.g., "mechanism for," "module for," "component for," "element for," "member for," "apparatus for," "machine for," "system for."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no fixed list; each term is fact-specific. Courts have found many such placeholders to invoke 112(f) (Welker Bearing, Mass. Inst. of Tech., Personalized Media, Mas-Hamilton). Examiners must consider the term in light of the specification and ordinary-art meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute/generic placeholder standard (Williamson)
rubrics_metrics.description: A substitute term acts as a generic placeholder when it would not be recognized by one of ordinary skill in the art as being sufficiently definite structure for performing the claimed function; the standard is whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Williamson and related cases explain that words like 'module' may be treated as non-structural. If POSA would not understand the term as the name of structure, 112(f) may apply even without the word 'means'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural terms that avoid 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms that connote structure (even if they identify structures by function) typically will not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f). Examples found not to invoke 112(f): "circuit," "detent mechanism," "digital detector," "reciprocating member," "connector assembly," "perforation," "sealingly connected joints," "eyeglass hanger member."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A term need not denote a specific physical structure to avoid 112(f); if POSA reads the term as sufficiently definite to name structure (as shown by specification, dictionaries, or prior art), 112(f) will not apply (Apex, CCS Fitness, Watts, Inventio AG).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural modifier precludes means-plus-function treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic placeholder preceded by a structural modifier (a term denoting a type of structural device) will not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'detent mechanism' was held not to invoke 112(f) because 'detent' denotes a known structural device. By contrast, non-structural modifiers (e.g., 'colorant selection mechanism' or 'distributed learning control module') may fail to impart structure and invoke 112(f). Examiners should check specification, dictionaries, and prior art to assess whether a modifier imparts structural meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional modification requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'means'/'step' or a generic placeholder must be modified by functional language for 112(f) to be implicated; the element must be set forth at least in part by the function it performs rather than specific structure/material/acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional linking words typically are 'for', 'so that', 'configured to', but other wording can suffice if it clearly recites a function. Mere use of 'means' without an associated function rebuts the presumption that 112(f) is invoked. Statements of function only in the preamble are generally insufficient to invoke 112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient structure/material/acts excludes 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim term is modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function, 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where structure precluded 112(f): 'baffle' with structure recited; 'positioning means for moving' where the claim provided list of structures; 'perforation means for tearing' where perforation structure is described. Conversely, sometimes similar terms have been held to invoke 112(f) (e.g., 'spring means'). Examiners should analyze whether claim recites definite structure for performing the function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-by-element applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies must be decided on an element-by-element basis; each claim must be independently reviewed even where similar language appears in other claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all words in a means-/step-plus-function clause are limited to the disclosed embodiment and equivalents because 112(f) applies only to the interpretation of the means/step that performs the recited function. Claims that are textually similar must be reviewed independently (O.I. Corp., IMS Technology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding structure must be disclosed in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding structure (or material or acts) of a means-/step-plus-function limitation must be disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure will perform the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure may be explicit, implicit/inherent, or in drawings if clear to POSA (Atmel, Dossel, Vas-Cath). A bare statement that known techniques can be used does not disclose structure for means-plus-function (Biomedino). The disclosure obligation ties to 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b): means-plus-function claiming limits claim scope to disclosed structure and equivalents, and failure to disclose adequate structure can render the claim indefinite or fail the written-description requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented means-plus-function: algorithm disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: For a computer-implemented 35 U.S.C. 112(f) claim limitation, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed specific computer function, or the claim is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When disclosed structure is a computer programmed to carry out an algorithm, the corresponding structure is that special-purpose computer programmed with the disclosed algorithm, not a general-purpose computer (NetMoneyIN, In re Aoyama, WMS Gaming). Examiners should look for an algorithm in the specification; absence may make the claim indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of inadequate corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is no disclosure of structure, material, or acts for performing the recited function, the claim fails to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefinite) and may also fail written-description/enablement requirements (112(a)/(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (Biomedino, Cardiac Pacemakers, Budde) illustrate that absence of disclosed corresponding structure can render means-plus-function claims indefinite or otherwise noncompliant. Examiners should consider whether the specification provides adequate structure, whether by text, drawings, or clear implication to POSA. Applicants may argue, amend, or supply clarifying disclosure where procedurally available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action and applicant response procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must expressly state application of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) in the Office action when applicable, and must explain reasons when a 'means'/'step' term is not treated under 112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In response to an Office action finding 112(f) invoked, applicant may (1) present a sufficient showing that the claim limitation recites sufficient structure to avoid 112(f), or (2) amend the claim limitation to avoid 112(f) (e.g., by reciting sufficient structure). If applicant disagrees with an examiner's interpretation, applicant may present arguments and amend to clarify whether 112(f) applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-specific nature and no absolutes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no absolute rules or fixed lists of words that always result in or always avoid 35 U.S.C. 112(f); every case turns on its own facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must carefully consider claim language in light of the specification and commonly accepted meaning in the technological art. Examples given are fact-specific and should not be applied as per se rules (Signtech, Seal-Flex, Mas-Hamilton, etc.).
